strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution by examining language-associated differences in descriptions of identical images. This focus has practical implications for caption collection, annotator metadata, and evaluation, independently of whether it produces benchmark-leading performance.

The investigation combines human Crossmodal-3600 captions, LLaVA outputs, and Vertex outputs across up to seven languages. The clear organization into semantic content, expression, embeddings, and fine-tuning provides complementary perspectives, while comparisons hold images and caption counts fixed.

The grounding and human experiments strengthen the descriptive finding. Table 3 reports Vertex object coverage against Visual Genome increasing from 9.6% for three English captions to 11.7% for English–French–Chinese captions. The separate study with 20 participants and 30 images reports 8.4% more scene-graph objects when combining English and Japanese descriptions.

Translation quality receives meaningful scrutiny: 15 native speakers give an average rating of 4.68/5, with additional checks on preservation of visual concepts. The manuscript also explicitly acknowledges limitations of language as a cultural proxy and the risk of cultural essentialism.
weaknesses: The cultural-perception interpretation is stronger than the experimental identification supports. Caption differences can reflect linguistic conventions, verbosity, annotation practices, and perceptual attention. The English–Japanese study does not separate these explanations because language and participant country vary together. Likewise, source-matched fine-tuning performance establishes adaptation to caption distributions, without independently demonstrating richer visual understanding. The supported conclusion is primarily about language-associated descriptions.

The translation controls do not validate every measurement. Preserving objects and relations does not establish preservation of LIWC authenticity, clout, or tone in translated short captions. The near-chance language classifier on sentence embeddings also cannot rule out translation artifacts that its representation or linear classifier fails to detect. Consequently, the manner-of-expression conclusions are less secure than the semantic-content findings.

Larger scene-graph unions are not fully established as additional correct visual information. Caption counts are matched, but no length-matched analysis is reported. The Visual Genome check measures object recall without corresponding precision or hallucination rates, and does not similarly validate the additional relations and attributes. These omissions limit interpretation of the coverage gains, particularly for generated captions.

Statistical support and reproducibility are incomplete. The principal coverage results, human-study effects, and fine-tuning comparisons lack uncertainty estimates or clearly specified significance procedures. Exact model/API versions, generation settings, fine-tuning hyperparameters, and scene-graph merging thresholds are insufficiently documented. These details matter for replicating the measurements and assessing small SPICE differences.

Several numerical statements require reconciliation. Table 1 reports a Vertex monolingual attribute average of 1.98 although every constituent value lies between 1.59 and 1.86; their mean is approximately 1.69. Table 11 identifies multilingual training as best on mixed evaluation, whereas Table 17 reports 0.154 for French training versus 0.151 for multilingual training. These reporting errors do not negate the repeated descriptive pattern, but reduce confidence in the exact gains and training conclusions. The worthwhile empirical evidence, balanced against unresolved measurement validity and reporting reliability, places the submission at the acceptance boundary.
